title: Trump Announced Major Iran Combat Operations in an Eight-Minute Truth Social Video
description_medium: On February 28, 2026, President Donald Trump announced that U.S. forces had begun “major combat operations in Iran” in an eight-minute video posted to Truth Social. He described the objective as eliminating imminent threats from Iran, including its nuclear program, missiles and naval forces, and called on Iranians to take over their government. Trump warned that American service members could be killed, framing the operation as a long-term security mission. The address set out the administration’s public case as the strikes began.
description_long: President Donald Trump announced the start of U.S. military action against Iran through an eight-minute video posted to his Truth Social account on February 28, 2026. The Associated Press published the statement in full. Trump said the military had begun “major combat operations” and described the objective as defending Americans by eliminating what he called imminent threats from the Iranian government. He pointed to Iran’s nuclear and missile programs, attacks attributed to Tehran and its regional proxies, and threats to U.S. forces and allies. He said U.S. forces would destroy Iranian missiles and their industry, target the navy, weaken proxy groups and prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The speech also addressed audiences inside Iran. Trump told members of the Revolutionary Guard, armed forces and police to lay down their weapons, promising immunity if they did so and threatening death otherwise. He told Iranians to stay sheltered during the attacks and said the opportunity to take control of their future was near. Trump acknowledged that U.S. personnel could be killed or wounded, presenting the operation as a mission to protect future generations from a nuclear-armed Iran. The address established the administration’s stated rationale and announced military objectives at the outset of the campaign; it did not include a live question-and-answer session or a detailed timetable for ending the operation.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump Announced Major Iran Combat Operations in a Pre-Recorded Social Video
corrected_wording.proposed_title: Trump Announced Major Iran Combat Operations in an Eight-Minute Truth Social Video
corrected_wording.reason: The reporting confirms the platform, duration and announcement, but does not establish whether the video was pre-recorded.

source_access_notes: Read the Associated Press statement publication syndicated by Boston.com.
rationale: Kept the documented video announcement while replacing the unsupported production detail and expanding the stated objectives and direct appeals.

title: Khamenei’s Killing Raised Immediate Questions About Iran’s Leadership and War’s Scope
description_medium: The U.S.-Israeli attack that killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei created an immediate leadership crisis and raised the risk of wider regional conflict. President Donald Trump said the killing gave Iranians a chance to take back their country, while Iranian state media confirmed his death. The Associated Press noted the stakes for an administration whose president had campaigned on an “America First” agenda and promises to avoid prolonged wars. The event left Iran’s political future uncertain as military operations continued.
description_long: The opening U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, a development that sharply widened the stakes of the military campaign. Iranian state media confirmed his death early Sunday after President Donald Trump had announced it and urged Iranians to take back their country. Khamenei had led the Islamic Republic since 1989, and his death placed the country’s political future in doubt. The Associated Press reported that the strike carried a risk of retaliation and a wider regional war, while also highlighting the tension between the scale of the intervention and Trump’s “America First” political identity. Trump had repeatedly portrayed himself as opposed to “forever wars”; now the United States was undertaking an operation that targeted Iran’s senior leadership as well as military and critical infrastructure. The administration publicly justified the strikes as necessary to confront imminent threats, particularly Iran’s nuclear and missile programs. The immediate question was whether killing the supreme leader would bring a political transition or instead intensify conflict. AP’s contemporaneous account noted that the future of the Islamic Republic was uncertain and that retaliatory violence could expand the war. These facts raised questions about the likely scope and consequences of the intervention, but they did not establish the administration’s ultimate political objective or demonstrate that the operation had already produced a change in Iranian governance.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump's Escalation Narrative Faced New Legitimacy Questions After Regime-Level Shock Reports
corrected_wording.proposed_title: Khamenei’s Killing Raised Immediate Questions About Iran’s Leadership and War’s Scope
corrected_wording.reason: The supplied coverage establishes the leadership shock and risk of regional instability, but not a measured change in the legitimacy of Trump’s narrative.

source_access_notes: Used the AP search excerpt for its same-day Khamenei report and read AP’s March 1 war-analysis report syndicated by WTOP. The linked CNN piece is dated August 6 and was not used for this February event.
rationale: Focused the entry on the documented leadership shock and reported risk of regional instability, without treating later August reporting as contemporaneous proof of legitimacy effects.

title: Iran War Put Trump’s Anti-Intervention Message Under Strain as Lawmakers Split on Risks
description_medium: The opening Iran strikes placed Trump’s long-standing opposition to foreign entanglements beside a new U.S. war. Associated Press reporting on March 1 documented sharply different reactions: Senator Lindsey Graham defended the campaign as consistent with “America First,” while Senators Mark Warner and Mark Kelly warned that it could become a sustained regional conflict and demanded a strategy. The debate showed that support for Trump’s decision did not erase concerns about duration, escalation and congressional oversight.
description_long: When the United States entered the war with Iran, the decision collided with Donald Trump’s repeated pledges to avoid foreign entanglements and focus on the Western Hemisphere. Associated Press reporting on March 1 described the intervention as a break from that rhetoric, while also showing that Republicans and Democrats offered sharply different readings of what “America First” meant. Republican Senator Lindsey Graham argued that the policy did not require isolationism and defended the use of force against threats to U.S. interests. Senator Tom Cotton predicted that elected Republicans and voters would support Trump. Democratic senators raised concerns about the path ahead. Mark Warner warned that the opening strikes could become a sustained regional war; Mark Kelly said he wanted to see a strategy and did not want a wider conflict; Tim Kaine called for Congress to vote on the action. AP also reported that some regional diplomats believed the United States and Israel had acted while diplomacy remained possible and feared escalation. The debate therefore involved both a challenge to Trump’s anti-war political identity and a disagreement over whether the operation was necessary, authorized and limited. The contemporaneous reporting documents competing arguments, not a collapse of the Republican coalition or a measured loss of public support. The immediate political question was whether the administration could explain how the attack fit its campaign commitments and what would prevent the conflict from expanding.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump's Coalition Faced Internal Identity Shock as Anti-War Messaging Collapsed
corrected_wording.proposed_title: Iran War Put Trump’s Anti-Intervention Message Under Strain as Lawmakers Split on Risks
corrected_wording.reason: The same-day AP account supports a tension with Trump’s prior rhetoric and documented debate, but not a collapse of movement coherence or a coalition-wide identity shock.

source_access_notes: Read the March 1 Associated Press report syndicated by WTOP. The linked BBC coalition analysis is dated March 14 and was not used to describe this March 1 entry.
rationale: Recast the claimed coalition collapse as the documented immediate debate, naming lawmakers’ contrasting positions and preserving the distinction between rhetoric and proven political effects.

title: Trump Took the United States Into Iran War Despite His Stated Aversion to Foreign Entanglements
description_medium: President Donald Trump’s decision to join attacks on Iran came despite decades of stated aversion to foreign entanglements and repeated promises to focus on the Western Hemisphere. In its March 1 account, the Associated Press reported that the administration described the strikes as a response to imminent threats, even though advisers had not identified a specific danger requiring urgent action. Lawmakers then disputed whether the campaign could remain limited or become a sustained regional war.
description_long: The Associated Press framed the opening Iran strikes as a sharp test of Donald Trump’s long-standing opposition to foreign entanglements. Trump had repeatedly promised an “America First” agenda focused primarily on the Western Hemisphere and had criticized prolonged U.S. wars. Yet over the weekend of February 28 and March 1, he joined Israel in attacks on Iran’s leadership, military and critical infrastructure. The administration’s stated justification was that Iran posed imminent risks to U.S. and allied interests. AP reported that even Trump’s closest advisers had not pointed to a specific Iranian threat requiring urgent action, and noted that the president had previously said a June strike had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear capability. The decision also raised questions about what would follow the opening attack. Iran’s supreme leader and senior officials had been killed, creating a leadership vacuum that AP said could pull the United States into the kind of prolonged conflict Trump had said he wanted to avoid. Republican allies argued that using force against threats could still fit “America First.” Democratic lawmakers questioned the legal basis, asked for a strategy and warned that the operation could expand into a sustained regional war. The report documents the contrast between Trump’s earlier rhetoric and his choice to use military force, as well as uncertainty about the campaign’s duration. It does not quantify reputational costs or show how allies and adversaries interpreted the policy shift.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump's Mideast Intervention Undermined His Claim to Be the Predictable Anti-War Alternative
corrected_wording.proposed_title: Trump Took the United States Into Iran War Despite His Stated Aversion to Foreign Entanglements
corrected_wording.reason: The AP report supports a contrast with his repeated anti-entanglement statements; it does not establish how allies or adversaries assessed predictability.

source_access_notes: Read the March 1 Associated Press report syndicated by WTOP. The linked CNN article is from August and was not used for this event account.
rationale: Kept the evidence-backed contrast with Trump’s past statements and removed unmeasured claims about reputational effects and misread risk.

title: Trump Warned Force Was Possible in Iran Talks One Day Before U.S. Strikes Began
description_medium: On February 27, after U.S.-Iran nuclear talks in Geneva ended without a deal, President Donald Trump said he was unhappy with the negotiations but had not made a final decision on military action. He said more discussions were expected and that he would prefer not to use force, though “sometimes you have to.” The following day, he announced that U.S. forces had begun major combat operations in Iran. The sequence marked a rapid shift from ongoing diplomacy to military action.
description_long: U.S.-Iran nuclear negotiations in Geneva ended without an agreement on February 26, 2026. The next day, President Donald Trump publicly expressed frustration with the talks but said he had not made a final decision on using military force. Reuters reported that he said additional discussions were expected and quoted him saying he would prefer not to use force, “but sometimes you have to.” Oman’s foreign minister, who mediated the negotiations, said significant progress had been made and argued that a deal remained within reach if diplomacy had room to continue. The diplomatic setting was accompanied by a substantial U.S. military presence in the region, including two aircraft carrier groups. Trump’s remarks therefore left open two possible paths: continued negotiation or an attack. On February 28, he announced in a Truth Social video that the U.S. military had begun “major combat operations” in Iran. The timing made the contrast between the public discussion of further talks and the start of combat especially stark. The sequence does not by itself show that Trump had promised to continue negotiations indefinitely or that his position was internally inconsistent; it shows that he publicly left the military option open one day before ordering an operation. The U.S. and Iranian accounts of the nuclear dispute also differed: Washington sought commitments against a weapons program, while Tehran denied seeking nuclear weapons and called for sanctions relief. The reporting places the attack in the context of a failed round of talks, renewed diplomatic contacts and military pressure already in place.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump's Iran Talk Stance Became a Pre-War Contradiction Once Combat Expanded Days Later
corrected_wording.proposed_title: Trump Warned Force Was Possible in Iran Talks One Day Before U.S. Strikes Began
corrected_wording.reason: Contemporaneous reporting establishes the one-day sequence and that Trump left force as an option, but not that combat represented a contradiction or that it expanded only days later.

source_access_notes: Read Reuters’ February 27 report and the AP statement publication syndicated by Boston.com. The supplied Reuters article about shifting war aims is dated March 20 and was not used to establish the February 27 sequence.
rationale: Changed the claim of contradiction to a chronological account that reflects Trump’s reported statements before the operation was announced.
